questions.title: Define normalisation
questions.text: Define the term **normalisation**.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Organising data into well-structured / related tables following rules (normal forms) (1)
- to reduce data redundancy / avoid anomalies / improve integrity (1)
scheme.model_answer: The process of organising a database into related tables by following the rules of the normal forms, so that redundancy is reduced and anomalies are avoided.

questions.title: The normal forms
questions.text: Match each normal form to its rule.

right.text: All values are atomic and there are no repeating groups
No non-key field depends on only part of a composite key
No non-key field depends on another non-key field

scheme.mark_scheme: 1NF–R1, 2NF–R2, 3NF–R3. One mark per correct match.

questions.title: Anomalies
questions.text: In a single table `Orders(OrderID, CustomerName, CustomerAddress, Product)`, match each problem to the type of anomaly.

left.text: A new customer cannot be stored until they place an order
A customer's address must be changed in every one of their orders
Deleting a customer's only order also deletes the customer's address

scheme.mark_scheme: L1–Insertion, L2–Update, L3–Deletion. One mark per correct match.

questions.title: Benefits of normalisation
questions.text: State **two** benefits of normalising a database.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each): reduced data redundancy / less repeated data; less storage; data consistency / integrity; no update / insertion / deletion anomalies; easier to maintain
scheme.model_answer: 1 Less repeated data. 2 A change only needs to be made in one place, so the data stays consistent.

questions.title: Atomic values
questions.text: A field `Phones` containing "87011112233, 87775554411" is acceptable in first normal form.

scheme.mark_scheme: False.
scheme.explanation: The field holds two values, so it is not atomic and breaks 1NF.

questions.title: Why not 1NF
questions.text:
| MovieID | Title | Year | Country |
|---|---|---|---|
| M1 | The Nomad | 2005 | Kazakhstan, France |
| M2 | Tulpan | 2008 | Kazakhstan, Germany |

Explain why the table is not in first normal form.

scheme.mark_scheme: Data in column Country is not atomic / Country field has multiple values (1). Accept answers only with the specified field name.
scheme.model_answer: The Country field contains more than one value in a cell, so it is not atomic.

questions.title: Bring to 1NF
questions.text: Describe how the table in the previous question can be changed into first normal form, and state the new primary key.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- One row for each film–country pair / one country per record (or a separate MovieCountries table) (1)
- primary key (MovieID, Country) (1)
scheme.model_answer: Store one country in each row, repeating the film for each country, so the primary key becomes (MovieID, Country).

questions.title: Partial dependency
questions.text: `Results(StudentID, SubjectID, StudentName, Mark)` has the composite key (StudentID, SubjectID). Explain why the table is not in second normal form.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- StudentName depends only on StudentID, which is part of the key (1)
- a partial dependency — 2NF requires every non-key field to depend on the whole key (1)

points.criterion: StudentName depends on part of the key

scheme.model_answer: StudentName depends only on StudentID, not on the whole key (StudentID, SubjectID); this partial dependency breaks 2NF.

questions.title: Transitive dependency
questions.text: `Employees(EmployeeID, Name, DeptID, DeptName)` has primary key EmployeeID. Explain why the table is not in third normal form.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- DeptName depends on DeptID, a non-key field (1)
- this transitive dependency breaks 3NF / DeptName should be in a Departments table (1)
scheme.model_answer: DeptName depends on DeptID, which is not the key; this transitive dependency breaks 3NF, so departments should be stored in their own table.

questions.title: Which normal form?
questions.text: Each table has the stated problem. Tick (✓) the **first** normal form that the table breaks.

prefill: With key (OrderID, ProductID), ProductName depends only on ProductID
With key CourseID, TeacherPhone depends on TeacherName

questions.title: Single-field keys and 2NF
questions.text: A table in first normal form whose primary key is a single field is automatically in second normal form.

scheme.mark_scheme: True.
scheme.explanation: Partial dependencies are only possible when the key has more than one field.

questions.title: Bring to 3NF
questions.text:
The following table is given. Bring it to third normal form (3NF).

| CourseName | TeacherName | DateOfBirth |
|---|---|---|
| Java | Karimov Arman | 12/03/1985 |
| Python | Karimov Arman | 12/03/1985 |
| Web design | Sadykova Aigerim | 04/11/1990 |

scheme.mark_scheme:
Define "Course" table with primary key (1)
Define "Teacher" table with primary key (1)
Define the relationship by indicating a foreign key (1)
[Max 3]
scheme.model_answer:
Teachers(TeacherID, TeacherName, DateOfBirth) — primary key TeacherID.
Courses(CourseID, CourseName, TeacherID) — primary key CourseID, foreign key TeacherID.

questions.title: Normalise an order table
questions.text:
Normalise the table below to 3NF. Show the tables with their primary keys and foreign keys.

`Orders ( OrderID, OrderDate, CustomerID, CustomerName, CustomerPhone )`

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Identifies that CustomerName / CustomerPhone depend on CustomerID (transitive) (1)
- Customers(CustomerID, CustomerName, CustomerPhone) with PK CustomerID (1)
- Orders(OrderID, OrderDate, CustomerID) with PK OrderID (1)
- CustomerID as a foreign key in Orders (1)
scheme.model_answer: CustomerName and CustomerPhone depend on CustomerID, not on OrderID. Customers(CustomerID, CustomerName, CustomerPhone) — PK CustomerID. Orders(OrderID, OrderDate, CustomerID) — PK OrderID, FK CustomerID.

questions.title: Moving fields
questions.text:
Complete the sentences.

When fields are moved into a new table, the field they depend on becomes the [[1]] key of the new table and stays in the original table as a [[2]] key.

scheme.mark_scheme: (1) primary (2) foreign

questions.title: Create linked tables
questions.text:
Write SQL to create the normalised tables:

```text
Teachers ( TeacherID, TeacherName )
Courses  ( CourseID, CourseName, TeacherID )
```

Include the primary keys and the foreign key.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- CREATE TABLE Teachers with TeacherID PRIMARY KEY and TeacherName with data types (1)
- CREATE TABLE Courses with CourseID PRIMARY KEY (1)
- CourseName and TeacherID with suitable data types (1)
- TeacherID REFERENCES Teachers(TeacherID) / FOREIGN KEY clause (1)
scheme.ai_instructions: Accept any reasonable data types and dialect.

questions.text:
| PupilID | PupilName | Class | ClassTeacher | Clubs |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| P1 | Dana | 11A | Mr Omarov | Chess, Robotics |
| P2 | Timur | 11B | Ms Ivanova | Chess |
| P3 | Aru | 11A | Mr Omarov | Robotics, Debate |

parts.title: 1NF problem
parts.text: Explain why the table is not in 1NF.

scheme.mark_scheme: The Clubs field contains multiple values / is not atomic (1)
scheme.model_answer: The Clubs field holds a list of clubs, so it is not atomic.

parts.title: Transitive dependency
parts.text: Identify the transitive dependency in the data.

scheme.mark_scheme: ClassTeacher depends on Class (1)
scheme.model_answer: ClassTeacher depends on Class, not on PupilID.

parts.title: 3NF design
parts.text: Write the tables of a 3NF design, showing the primary and foreign keys.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Classes(Class, ClassTeacher) PK Class (1)
Pupils(PupilID, PupilName, Class) PK PupilID, FK Class (1)
Clubs(ClubID, ClubName) or club names in the link table (1)
Memberships(PupilID, ClubID) composite PK / both FKs (1)

Pupils(PupilID, PupilName, Class) — PK PupilID, FK Class
Clubs(ClubID, ClubName) — PK ClubID
Memberships(PupilID, ClubID) — composite PK, both FKs

questions.title: Explain normalisation
questions.text:
A clinic stores all its data in one table:

`Visits ( VisitID, VisitDate, PatientName, PatientPhone, DoctorName, DoctorRoom, Diagnosis )`

Explain the problems with this design and how normalisation to 3NF would solve them. Give the final tables with their keys.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Problems (max 2): patient / doctor details repeated — redundancy; update anomaly (phone / room change); insertion anomaly (new doctor with no visits); deletion anomaly
Normalisation (max 2): transitive dependencies — PatientPhone depends on patient, DoctorRoom on doctor; moved into separate tables
Final tables (max 2): Patients(PatientID, Name, Phone); Doctors(DoctorID, Name, Room); Visits(VisitID, VisitDate, PatientID*, DoctorID*, Diagnosis)
scheme.model_answer: Each visit repeats the patient's phone and the doctor's room, which wastes space; if a doctor changes room, every visit row must be updated, and a new doctor cannot be stored until he has a visit. PatientPhone depends on the patient and DoctorRoom on the doctor, not on VisitID — transitive dependencies. Normalising to 3NF moves these into separate tables: Patients(PatientID, Name, Phone), Doctors(DoctorID, Name, Room) and Visits(VisitID, VisitDate, PatientID, DoctorID, Diagnosis), where PatientID and DoctorID are foreign keys.

questions.title: The rules of normalisation
questions.text: A database designer normalises the tables of a new school system.

parts.title: Rules
parts.text: Draw a line to link each normal form to its rule.

right.text: Fields contain atomic values; no repeating groups
No partial dependencies on a composite key
No transitive dependencies between non-key fields

scheme.mark_scheme: 1NF–R1, 2NF–R2, 3NF–R3. One mark per line.

parts.title: Update anomaly
parts.text: Describe what is meant by an **update anomaly**.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- The same data is stored in several records (1)
- if it is changed in some records but not all, the data becomes inconsistent (1)
scheme.model_answer: When the same fact is stored in many rows, changing it in some rows but not others leaves the database inconsistent.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each): reduced redundancy; less storage; consistency / integrity; no anomalies; easier maintenance
scheme.model_answer: 1 Reduced data redundancy. 2 Data stays consistent.

parts.title: Partial dependency
parts.text: Explain what a **partial dependency** is, using an example.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- A non-key field depends on only part of a composite primary key (1)
- example, e.g. key (StudentID, SubjectID): StudentName depends only on StudentID (1)
scheme.model_answer: A non-key field that depends on only part of a composite key: with key (StudentID, SubjectID), StudentName depends only on StudentID.

questions.title: A library table
questions.text:
| BookID | Title | Authors | PublisherName | PublisherCity |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| B1 | Abai Zholy | M. Auezov | Zhazushy | Almaty |
| B2 | Kazakh Tales | A. Bekova, D. Ospan | Foliant | Astana |
| B3 | Steppe Songs | D. Ospan | Zhazushy | Almaty |

parts.title: Not 1NF
parts.text: Explain why the table is not in first normal form.

scheme.mark_scheme: Data in column Authors is not atomic / Authors field has multiple values (1). Accept only with the field name.
scheme.model_answer: The Authors field contains more than one author in one cell.

parts.title: Fix 1NF
parts.text: Describe how the Authors data should be stored to satisfy 1NF.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- One author per record / separate table BookAuthors / Authors linked to Books (1)
- with a composite key (BookID, AuthorID / Author) (1)

points.criterion: One author per record / separate table

scheme.model_answer: Store each author in a separate record of a BookAuthors table with the composite key (BookID, Author).

parts.title: Transitive dependency
parts.text: Identify the transitive dependency in the table and explain why it is a problem.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- PublisherCity depends on PublisherName, not on BookID (1)
- the city of each publisher is repeated for every book / update anomaly if a publisher moves (1)
scheme.model_answer: PublisherCity depends on PublisherName rather than on BookID, so Zhazushy's city is stored for every book it publishes and would have to be changed in many rows.

parts.title: 3NF design
parts.text: Write a 3NF design for this data, showing every table with its primary key and foreign keys.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Publishers(PublisherID, PublisherName, PublisherCity) — PK (1)
Books(BookID, Title, PublisherID) — PK BookID (1), FK PublisherID (1)
Authors(AuthorID, AuthorName) — PK (1)
BookAuthors(BookID, AuthorID) — composite PK / both FKs (1)
Accept author names stored directly in BookAuthors(BookID, AuthorName) for the last two marks.
scheme.model_answer:
Publishers(PublisherID, PublisherName, PublisherCity) — PK PublisherID
Books(BookID, Title, PublisherID) — PK BookID, FK PublisherID
Authors(AuthorID, AuthorName) — PK AuthorID
BookAuthors(BookID, AuthorID) — composite PK, both FKs

questions.text:

`Results ( StudentID, SubjectCode, StudentName, SubjectName, TeacherID, TeacherRoom, Mark )`

Each subject is taught by one teacher; each teacher has one room.

parts.text: Identify **two** partial dependencies in the table.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each): StudentName depends on StudentID; SubjectName depends on SubjectCode; TeacherID depends on SubjectCode
scheme.model_answer: 1 StudentName depends only on StudentID. 2 SubjectName depends only on SubjectCode.

parts.text: Write the tables in second normal form.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Students(StudentID, StudentName) (1)
Subjects(SubjectCode, SubjectName, TeacherID, TeacherRoom) (1)
Results(StudentID, SubjectCode, Mark) with composite key / FKs (1)

Subjects(SubjectCode, SubjectName, TeacherID, TeacherRoom)
Results(StudentID, SubjectCode, Mark)

parts.title: 3NF
parts.text: One of your 2NF tables is not in 3NF. Identify the problem and write the tables that bring it to 3NF.

- TeacherRoom depends on TeacherID, a non-key field in Subjects (transitive) (1)
- Teachers(TeacherID, TeacherRoom) (1)
- Subjects(SubjectCode, SubjectName, TeacherID) with FK TeacherID (1)

parts.title: SQL
parts.text: Write SQL to create the `Results` table with its composite primary key and foreign keys.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- CREATE TABLE Results with StudentID, SubjectCode, Mark and data types (1)
- PRIMARY KEY (StudentID, SubjectCode) (1)
- FOREIGN KEY references to Students and Subjects (1)

summary: Why databases are normalised, the rules for first, second and third normal form, how to normalise a table step by step to 3NF, and how to create a database with multiple related tables.

blocks.content: The process of **organising the data in a relational database into well-structured tables** — by following a set of rules called **normal forms** — so that each fact is stored **once**, data **redundancy** is reduced and **anomalies** (problems when inserting, updating or deleting data) are avoided.

blocks.title: Anomalies in an unnormalised table
columns: Example (one big *Orders* table with customer details in every row)
rows: **Update anomaly**
The same data is stored many times; changing it in one row but not others makes the data **inconsistent**
A customer's address must be changed in every order row
**Insertion anomaly**
Some data cannot be added without other unrelated data
A new customer cannot be stored until they place an order
**Deletion anomaly**
Deleting one record also deletes other important data
Deleting a customer's only order deletes the customer too

items.title: Benefits of normalisation
items.content:
- **Less redundancy** — less repeated data, less storage.
- **Data consistency / integrity** — each fact is changed in one place.
- **No anomalies** when inserting, updating or deleting.
- Clearer structure; easier to **maintain** and extend.

items.title: Possible drawback
items.content: - More tables means queries need **joins**, which can make some queries slower or more complex. (Very large systems sometimes **denormalise** a little for speed.)

theory.title: The rules of the normal forms

blocks.title: First, second and third normal form
rows: Every field contains **atomic (single) values**; there are **no repeating groups**; each record is **unique** (has a primary key)
One value per cell; no lists; no columns like `Phone1, Phone2, Phone3`
In **1NF**, and every non-key field depends on the **whole** primary key — **no partial dependencies**
Only matters when the primary key is **composite**: a field must not depend on just part of the key
In **2NF**, and **no non-key field depends on another non-key field** — **no transitive dependencies**
"Every non-key field depends on **the key, the whole key and nothing but the key**"

blocks.content: Field B **depends on** field A (A → B) if each value of A determines exactly one value of B. Example: `StudentID → StudentName` (knowing the ID tells you the name).

blocks.title: Types of dependency
rows: **Full**
A non-key field depends on the **whole** (composite) key
`(StudentID, SubjectID) → Mark`
**Partial** (breaks 2NF)
A non-key field depends on **part** of a composite key
`(StudentID, SubjectID) → StudentName`, but `StudentName` depends only on `StudentID`
**Transitive** (breaks 3NF)
A non-key field depends on **another non-key field**
`StudentID → ClassID → ClassTeacher`

blocks.title: A table that is not in 1NF
blocks.content:
| MovieID | Title | Year | Country |
|---|---|---|---|
| M1 | The Nomad | 2005 | Kazakhstan, France |
| M2 | Tulpan | 2008 | Kazakhstan, Germany, Russia |

The field **Country** is **not atomic** — it holds **several values**. Searching for "all films made in Germany" or counting films per country is difficult and error-prone.

blocks.title: Converting to 1NF
items: Make every field **atomic**: one value per cell (split multi-value fields; split `FullName` into `FirstName` and `Surname` if needed).
Remove **repeating groups** (columns such as `Country1, Country2…`).
Ensure each record is unique with a **primary key**.

blocks.title: The same data in 1NF — one row per film–country pair
blocks.content:
| MovieID | Title | Year | Country |
|---|---|---|---|
| M1 | The Nomad | 2005 | Kazakhstan |
| M1 | The Nomad | 2005 | France |
| M2 | Tulpan | 2008 | Kazakhstan |
| M2 | Tulpan | 2008 | Germany |
| M2 | Tulpan | 2008 | Russia |

Primary key: **(MovieID, Country)**. The table is now in 1NF, but `Title` and `Year` are **repeated** — they depend only on `MovieID`, which is **part** of the key → not yet 2NF.
If a field mixes two kinds of information, such as `Country = "Kazakhstan, Almaty"`, split it into **two atomic fields** `Country` and `City`.

blocks.title: Converting from 1NF to 2NF
items: Identify the **primary key**. If it is a **single field**, a table in 1NF is **already in 2NF**.
If the key is **composite**, check each non-key field: does it depend on the **whole** key or only **part** of it?
Move every field that depends on **only part** of the key into a **new table**, with that part of the key as its primary key.
Keep the part of the key in the original table as a **foreign key**.

blocks.title: 2NF — splitting the films table
blocks.content:
```text
Movies         ( _MovieID_, Title, Year )
MovieCountries ( _MovieID*_, _Country_ )
```
`Title` and `Year` now depend on the whole key of `Movies`. `MovieCountries` has only key fields. Both tables are in **2NF**.

blocks.title: Converting from 2NF to 3NF
items: Look for a **non-key field that depends on another non-key field** (a transitive dependency).
Move those fields into a **new table**; the field they depend on becomes the **primary key** of the new table.
Leave that field in the original table as a **foreign key**.

blocks.title: A table in 2NF but not 3NF
blocks.content:
| CourseName | TeacherName | TeacherDateOfBirth |
|---|---|---|
| Java | Karimov Arman | 12/03/1985 |
| Python | Karimov Arman | 12/03/1985 |
| Web design | Sadykova Aigerim | 04/11/1990 |

Primary key: `CourseName`. `TeacherDateOfBirth` depends on **TeacherName**, not on the course → **transitive dependency** (`CourseName → TeacherName → TeacherDateOfBirth`). Karimov's date of birth is stored twice.

blocks.title: The same data in 3NF
blocks.content:
```text
Teachers ( _TeacherID_, TeacherName, DateOfBirth )
Courses  ( _CourseID_, CourseName, TeacherID* )
```
| TeacherID | TeacherName | DateOfBirth |
|---|---|---|
| T1 | Karimov Arman | 12/03/1985 |
| T2 | Sadykova Aigerim | 04/11/1990 |

| CourseID | CourseName | TeacherID |
|---|---|---|
| C1 | Java | T1 |
| C2 | Python | T1 |
| C3 | Web design | T2 |

Each fact is stored **once**; the relationship is **Teachers 1 — M Courses** through the foreign key `TeacherID`.

blocks.title: Unnormalised data — a school's club register
blocks.content:
| PupilID | PupilName | Class | ClassTeacher | Clubs |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| P1 | Dana | 11A | Mr Omarov | Chess, Robotics |
| P2 | Timur | 11B | Ms Ivanova | Chess |
| P3 | Aru | 11A | Mr Omarov | Robotics, Debate |

blocks.title: Step by step
rows: `Clubs` contains lists
`PupilClubs(PupilID, PupilName, Class, ClassTeacher, Club)` with key **(PupilID, Club)**
`PupilName`, `Class`, `ClassTeacher` depend only on `PupilID` (part of the key)
`Pupils(PupilID, PupilName, Class, ClassTeacher)` and `Memberships(PupilID*, Club)`
`ClassTeacher` depends on `Class`, a non-key field
`Classes(Class, ClassTeacher)`; `Pupils(PupilID, PupilName, Class*)`; `Memberships(PupilID*, Club)`

blocks.content:
Classes     ( _Class_, ClassTeacher )
Pupils      ( _PupilID_, PupilName, Class* )
Clubs       ( _ClubID_, ClubName )
Memberships ( _PupilID*_, _ClubID*_ )

theory.title: Creating a database with multiple tables

blocks.title: From the normalised design to a working database
items: Create a table for each entity in the 3NF design, with the correct **data types** (from the data dictionary).
Set each table's **primary key** (composite where needed).
Create the **foreign keys** and the **relationships** between tables, with **referential integrity**.
Enter test data — first in the "one" tables, then in the "many" tables.
Test with **queries** that join the tables.

blocks.caption: Creating the normalised tables in SQL

blocks.title: Exam-style answers
blocks.content:
**Q: Explain why the Movie table is not in first normal form. [1]**
The data in the column **Country** is **not atomic** — the Country field has **multiple values**. *(Name the field.)*

**Q: Bring the Movie table to the first normal form. [1]**
Split the field into atomic values, e.g. add a **City** column: `Movies (MovieID, Title, Year, Genre, Duration, Country, City)`.

**Q: Bring the table (CourseName, TeacherName, DateOfBirth) to third normal form. [3]**
Define a **Course** table with a primary key (1); define a **Teacher** table with a primary key (1); define the **relationship** with a **foreign key** (`TeacherID` in Course) (1).

**Q: List the rule for second normal form. [1]**
The table is in 1NF and every non-key field depends on the **whole** primary key (**no partial dependencies**).

- Saying a table is "not in 1NF" without naming the **field** and the problem.
- Thinking 2NF matters for single-field keys — a 1NF table with a **single-field key** is automatically in 2NF.
- Forgetting to leave a **foreign key** behind when moving fields to a new table — the tables can no longer be linked.
- Splitting tables so much that data is **lost** — every original fact must still be stored.
- Confusing a **partial** dependency (2NF) with a **transitive** one (3NF).
